items.headline: 烏克蘭無人機襲俄境
items.context: 烏克蘭近期持續以長程無人機打擊俄羅斯境內目標。俄羅斯官員通報，別爾哥羅德（Belgorod）一起攻擊造成6人死亡；另有官員說，一起深入俄羅斯境內的攻擊造成至少13人死亡、75人受傷，是俄烏開戰以來最慘重的無人機攻擊之一。
items.thread_text:
烏克蘭近期持續以長程無人機打擊俄羅斯境內目標，多個城市傳出傷亡。

—— 本則整理自 Reuters、NPR、BBC 於 2026 年 8 月 10、11 日發佈的報導，讓圖書館員翻譯給你聽。

items.headline: 納坦雅胡拒加薩和平案
items.context: 以色列總理納坦雅胡（Benjamin Netanyahu）駁回川普提出的加薩和平方案，要求哈瑪斯先解除武裝才能談。這距離川普宣布已與哈瑪斯達成「歷史性協議」，還不到兩週。美方目前把這次拒絕當作以色列大選前的政治語言，並不特別緊張。
items.thread_text:
以色列總理納坦雅胡（Benjamin Netanyahu）拒絕川普提出的加薩和平方案，要求哈瑪斯先解除武裝才能談。

這距離川普宣布已與哈瑪斯達成「歷史性協議」還不到兩週。美國政府目前把這次拒絕視為以色列大選前的政治語言，反應相對平淡；但加薩當地巴勒斯坦人則擔心，沒有以色列撤軍、重建與保證，和平恐怕還是遙遙無期。

sources.summary: Assembly Roxy, Edinburgh A researcher encounters an isolated community in thrall to a mysterious religious leader in Jack MacGregor’s atmospheric but elusive drama What impresses about Jack MacGregor as a playwright is their willingness to take us into the wider world. Nightlands was set in a deserted Russian research base in Svalbard; Everything Under the Sun concerned militias in Mali; and Our Brother played out in the Cambodia of Pol Pot. So it is with Prophets, which begins with the arrival of Kerris, a Scottish researcher, on the sparsely populated island of Saint John, a fictional British Overseas Territory in the South Pacific. Played by Rebecca Wilkie, she is as curious about the religious activities of the islanders as she is the archaeological record of plant life she is supposedly there to study. Welcomed by Joe, a former merchant seaman played by a multitasking Xander Cowan, she senses something is amiss in the nightly church services led by an elusive man they call the prophet. Her job is about the dawn of time, but the locals are readying themselves for the end of days. Continue reading...
sources.title: Prophets review – a mysterious tale of faith at the end of the world

sources.summary: Royal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon This prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance During the RSC’s 65 years, numerous Lears have lost their minds and frequent Caesars been slaughtered by their courts. Now, though, a tyrant new to its stages faces both fates. He is King Aerys II Targaryen, ancestor of one warring bloodline in Game of Thrones , the dramatisation of George RR Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire series of fantasy novels that helped TV streamers’ rise to global domination during eight HBO seasons from 2011 to 2019. Some may balk at an institution named for England’s greatest dramatist staging an American drama franchise. There is, though, a compelling economic imperative: rising costs due to current wars (a frequent problem for Martin’s ancient oligarchs too) and Covid-era debts now exacerbated by paying back government loans means that the RSC could use another big commercial transfer – as its musical Matilda may not be immortal. sources.summary: When discontented Lily becomes a fantastical sea creature her low-budget transformation is strikingly unconvincing, rather in tune with the whole film Mermaidcore comes to the Welsh coastline in this somewhat stilted family movie about a teenager called Lily who turns into a mermaid. You could imagine it being developed into a series for kids’ TV but as a film it unfortunately falls at the first hurdle – failing to pull off a convincing mermaid transformation. Poor Lily’s shimmering tail is very obviously made from nylon that becomes very clingy when wet, making her legs very visible under the scales. Ellie Bindman plays Lily, who has moved from London to the Welsh seaside with her family for her stepdad’s work. Resentful about leaving her friends, she is huffy, communicating with her mum Claire (Marie Wilson) primarily in eyerolls. Lily’s only friend in town is Shane (Jack Taruschio Thomas), an awkward, slightly odd trainee local reporter who is following a lead about a mermaid sighting. One day Lily finds a glistening shell on the beach that transforms her into a mermaid and off she swims, tail arcing in the water. Continue reading...

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Combining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journey ‘But after all, writing is nothing more than a guided dream,” wrote Jorge Luis Borges. Dreams and dreaming are fertile concerns for Rosalind Belben, too. Her fourth book, originally published in 1979 and reissued last yea r, was titled Dreaming of Dead People. It was followed, a decade later, by Is Beauty Good. Now available in a new edition from the Sheffield indie And Other Stories, this eccentric polyphonic novel contains dozens of considerations of dreams, including dogs’ dreams and horses’ dreams as well as human beings’. Yet what makes it extraordinary is Belben’s ability to capture in words the slippery state that is neither dreaming nor sleeping nor waking, but somewhere in the edgelands between all three. “I fall awake and think, I want to go home. But there is no home.” So begins the chapter entitled Exile, a deliciously elusive story that is, most of the time at least, narrated in the first person by someone who is probably a woman, “a grizzled, cropped person”, and probably quite old and alone. They might be travelling through mountains somewhere, perhaps on a bus. They aren’t sure: “I am quite lost, wherever I am. I want to surrender. I wish to retire. I am tired.” Swishing about are uncertain memories of a childhood “shrouded” in nightmares: there was an orchard with an abundance of flora and fauna, and larks and swallows and “swifts to scream”. Like the author, the narrator was “born in the mud month” of February, and longs to disappear into marshlands to “be touched and stroked by plants”. But Belben never lets us rest in one place for long. Slipping in and out of sleep, “suffering glimpses”, the narrator stares at “a pink and blue angel” in the plaster of the wall. Which wall, you wonder, and how did we get here? This is the lure of Belben’s hypnagogia, the dizzying space into which she writes. Continue reading...
sources.title: Is Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben review – the literary equivalent of free jazz
